To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic administration of L-arginine methyl-ester (L-NAME), a nonselective inhibitor of nitric oxide synthases, to rats causes hypertension and renal injury.
dietary doses of inorganic nitrite restore the circulating nitric oxide levels and improve renal injury induced by L-NAME in rats.
dietary doses of inorganic nitrite restore circulating NO level and improve renal damage in L-NAME-treated hypertensive rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of dietary doses of nitrites on blood NO level and renal injury induced by L-NAME administration.
the role of nitrite as an NO donor in vivo and its potential as a novel therapeutic agent.
the role of nitrite as a NO precursor in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nitrite may be a potential candidate for the treatment of hypertension-induced renal disease.
the dietary nitrite-derived nitric oxide generation may be a backup system when nitric oxide synthases and L-arginine-dependent nitric oxide production systems are compromised.
dietary nitrite is a promising candidate as a therapeutic agent for hypertension and renal disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nitrite-derived NO is a promising therapeutic strategy for renal injury.
the NO generated from nitrite may serve as a protective factor against hypertension-induced renal damage.

The main takeaway from our work is that
nitrite may have a therapeutic potential for renal injury associated with chronic hypertension and renal failure.
